questions.q: What does Progress Iteratively With Feedback ask organizations to do instead of one sweeping initiative?
options: Organize work into smaller, manageable pieces completed in a timely manner
Freeze all improvement work until a single annual planning cycle
Delegate every decision to an external vendor for speed
Avoid measuring outcomes until the entire initiative is finished
questions.explain: The principle pushes toward comprehending the whole but acting in smaller, well-defined pieces rather than one large release.

questions.q: What is the main risk of a "big-bang" initiative, according to this lesson?
options: It costs slightly more in licensing fees than a phased rollout
It concentrates all of the project's risk into one release event, discovered only after most of the investment is spent
It requires more stakeholders to sign off than a phased rollout
It is always technically impossible to deliver
questions.explain: If something is wrong with a big-bang plan, you typically don't find out until it's expensive to course-correct, since the risk wasn't spread across checkpoints.

questions.q: Why is the "feedback" part of this principle's name not optional decoration?
options: Because feedback is only required when a project runs over budget
Because it's the mechanism that makes each iteration's outcome actually inform the plan for the next one
Because ITIL 4 requires a signed feedback form for every change
Because feedback is only relevant to software development, not ITSM
questions.explain: Without feedback changing the next iteration's plan, the loop isn't actually closed — you'd just be doing small releases without learning from them.

questions.q: How does this principle relate to Agile and Lean thinking?
options: It explicitly has no relationship to Agile or Lean concepts
It only applies to software teams, never to IT service management
It's explicitly aligned with Agile and Lean — short cycles, visible progress, and adjusting based on what's learned
It replaces Agile methods entirely within ITIL 4
questions.explain: ITIL 4 absorbed ideas from Agile software development, recognizing the same logic makes iterative service improvement safer too.

questions.q: Why does this principle depend on Start Where You Are to work well?
options: It doesn't depend on it at all; the two principles are unrelated
Because without first assessing the current state, you can't define a sensible first small piece of work to tackle
Because Start Where You Are requires finishing all iteration first
Because ITIL 4 lists principles strictly in the order they must be applied
questions.explain: Iterating without first assessing the current state just produces a series of small, uninformed guesses rather than a genuine feedback loop.
